voyages.name: HMS Beagle: selected ship itinerary, 1831–1836
voyages.summary: FitzRoy’s ship itinerary with selected dated ports and survey waypoints. Darwin’s inland journeys are excluded. Large gaps include repeated South American surveying; the line does not reproduce those cruises. Galápagos departure follows the ship on 20 October, not Darwin’s final shore visit on 17 October.

stops.note: Volume II, pp. 119–120. Arrival observation only; later departure is not specified here.

This is the source’s regional Centla reference for the land party, not a fleet anchorage or an exact battlefield boundary. Travel onward to San Juan de Ulúa is untraced.

stops.name: San Juan de Ulúa
stops.note: Díaz dates the arrival to Holy Thursday, 21 April in the historical Julian calendar. The party met emissaries of Motecuhzoma with interpretation by Malintzin.

stops.name: Cempoala
stops.note: The coastal expedition’s leaders left Cempoala with Indigenous allies and headed toward Tlaxcala after weeks of coastal movement and negotiation.

stops.name: Tlaxcalan capital area
stops.note: After warfare near the Tlaxcalan frontier, the troops accepted their hosts’ invitation to move to the area of the Tlaxcalan capitals. The approximate mark represents that cluster.

stops.name: Cholula
stops.note: Cortés’s troops and Tlaxcalan allies carried out a massacre in Cholula. The point marks presence in the city on the first dated day of the attack.

stops.name: Tenochtitlan
stops.note: The alliance entered the island city and Cortés met Motecuhzoma. The city marker is schematic.

voyages.name: Narváez’s fleet and Florida expedition
voyages.summary: Narváez left Spain with a colonizing fleet and wintered in Cuba after a storm damaged the expedition. The land force traveled from the Tampa Bay region into Apalachee and left the Gulf coast in improvised boats. Several sites and sections of the route remain uncertain.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda
stops.note: Narváez led five ships from Sanlúcar under royal orders to conquer and govern territory between Florida and the Río de las Palmas.

stops.name: Trinidad, Cuba, harbor vicinity
stops.note: Narváez reached Trinidad, where a severe storm wrecked vessels and destroyed supplies. Subsequent repairs and dispositions broke up the fleet.

stops.name: Xagua/Jagua Bay, Cuba
stops.note: Narváez arrived at Jagua after Cabeza de Vaca had wintered there with the force’s ships. The fleet subsequently sought a pilot and attempted to round Cuba’s western end.

stops.name: Florida coast, Tampa Bay approaches
stops.note: The narrative prints 12 April for the approach. Carson’s reconstruction gives Tuesday 7 April. The NPS places the landing near Tampa Bay. The marker denotes the approach region.

stops.name: Apalachee capital region, northwest Florida
stops.note: Cabeza de Vaca places the expedition within sight of Apalache on the day after the feast of St. John, 25 June. The mark identifies the regional destination. The precise village reached by Narváez remains unsettled.

stops.name: Bay of Horses / Apalachee Bay vicinity
stops.note: The survivors embarked in five boats after making them at the Bay of Horses. The point identifies the broad Apalachee Bay vicinity based on archaeological research. The exact embarkation site and the boats’ separate routes remain disputed.

voyages.name: Cabeza de Vaca and the survivors’ journey
voyages.summary: A dated Texas-coast event and a later departure in Sinaloa frame years of survival, confinement, travel and reliance on Indigenous communities. Andrés Dorantes, Alonso del Castillo and Estevanico survived with Cabeza de Vaca. The long gap represents disputed routes and shifting groups.
voyages.precision: Schematic regional observations. The wreck location and overland route between the Texas coast and Sinaloa remain disputed.

stops.name: Upper Texas coast, Malhado region
stops.note: Cabeza de Vaca’s boat came ashore on the island he called Malhado. Galveston and Follet’s Island are among proposed identifications. The marker shows the coast region without identifying a landfall point.

stops.name: San Miguel de Culiacán
stops.note: The four left San Miguel de Culiacán after reaching New Spain. They traveled to Compostela and eventually Mexico City. The dated anchor denotes departure from the Culiacán settlement area.

voyages.name: Cabeza de Vaca’s return to Europe
voyages.summary: Cabeza de Vaca traveled from New Spain to Lisbon following the Narváez expedition. The account records the Cuba stay and storms near Bermuda.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: Veracruz harbor area
stops.note: Cabeza de Vaca left Veracruz after an earlier return attempt failed. Dorantes was present at the departure but did not complete the return voyage.

stops.name: Havana
stops.note: The ship arrived at Havana on 4 May and waited until 2 June for expected ships before going on.

stops.name: Lisbon harbor
stops.note: He reached Lisbon after the Atlantic crossing. The narrative describes a storm near Bermuda and a later approach to the Azores.

voyages.name: De Soto’s Southeast expedition
voyages.summary: Selected points trace the expedition from Havana to Tampa Bay, Anhaica and Coosa, and end in the lower Mississippi region. Spanish demands produced dispossession, forced labor and Indigenous resistance. The Arkansas, Mabila and Chickasaw phases lack sufficiently precise junctions for a continuous map line.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: Havana harbor
stops.note: Elvas records nine vessels leaving Havana.

stops.name: Tampa Bay / Ucita landing area
stops.note: The force disembarked 30 May near the town of Ucita. The bay point is representative. The shore site is debated.

stops.name: Anhaica, Apalachee
stops.note: The expedition left its first winter encampment at the Apalachee capital, now archaeologically identified in Tallahassee. The date is the confirmed departure day.

stops.name: Coosa, Little Egypt site area
stops.note: The army departed the chief town of Coosa, identified with the submerged Little Egypt site near Carters Lake. Its earlier arrival differs between historical chronologies.

stops.name: Guachoya, lower Mississippi region
stops.note: Elvas places de Soto’s arrival at the town on 17 April and his death there on 21 May. The mark denotes the lower Mississippi reach in the NPS reconstruction. The town’s exact site is unsettled.

voyages.name: Moscoso’s withdrawal to New Spain
voyages.summary: After de Soto’s death, Luis de Moscoso led the surviving force west and returned to the Mississippi. The dated coastal anchors document the brigantines’ withdrawal and the terminal river entry. The many river bends, storms and landings are not resolved by these dates.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: Mississippi delta approaches
stops.note: The brigantines entered the Gulf of Mexico after leaving Minoya on 2 July and descending the Mississippi. The delta region has changed and the historic outlet is unsettled.

stops.name: Pánuco River mouth
stops.note: Elvas dates the survivors’ entry into the Pánuco River. After a storm scattered the brigantines, some survivors continued overland.

voyages.name: Coronado’s march to Háwikuh
voyages.summary: Coronado led the first part of his expedition from western New Spain into Zuni territory. The main body and distinct maritime support and scouting parties used other itineraries.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: Compostela, Nayarit
stops.note: Coronado’s force left Compostela with Spanish soldiers, many Indigenous allies and large herds. The day follows the National Park Service chronology.

stops.name: Culiacán
stops.note: The expedition reached Culiacán on Easter Sunday according to the published route study. The vanguard set out from the province on 22 April, according to Coronado’s letter.

stops.name: Los Corazones, Río Sonora region
stops.note: The advance party reached the Valley of Hearts. The location is a regional marker in the Río Sonora area used in the route scholarship. The exact trail in Sonora and across the upper Southwest remains debated.

stops.name: Háwikuh, Zuni
stops.note: The vanguard reached Háwikuh and forced the Zuni defenders to abandon the pueblo after a Spanish assault. Coronado used the pueblo as a headquarters while scouting parties left in several directions.

voyages.name: Pérez’s Santiago reconnaissance
voyages.summary: Juan José Pérez captained Santiago from New Spain to the Pacific Northwest. The voyage included encounters with Haida canoe crews in Dixon Entrance and with Nuu-chah-nulth traders off Nootka Sound. The archive and the Navy study differ on some July observations.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: Santiago sailed north from its naval base. It called at San Diego and Monterey before continuing north. Their outward day-level port stops are omitted here.

stops.name: Dixon Entrance, Haida Gwaii vicinity
stops.note: The Navy study identifies a 19 July anchorage near 54°25′ N in Dixon Entrance and describes Indigenous people approaching by canoe. The National Archives describes seeing land at Dixon Entrance on 15 July, a separate sighting.

stops.name: Off Nootka Sound
stops.note: Pérez anchored near the entrance to Nootka Sound. Indigenous visitors came to the Santiago from Yuquot. The Spanish crew stayed aboard. The coastwise leg to California has no intermediate day-level fix in this selection.

stops.name: Monterey Bay
stops.note: Santiago returned to Monterey for repairs before resuming the return voyage on 9 October.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: The ship reached San Blas after its southbound passage.

voyages.name: Heceta’s Santiago survey
voyages.summary: Santiago surveyed the California and Washington coasts with Sonora before the vessels separated. On the southbound leg Heceta identified the mouth of the Columbia River from offshore.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: The naval expedition sailed from San Blas. The initial departure was followed by a delay and changes in command.

stops.name: Trinidad Bay coast, California
stops.note: The vessels sighted the California coast and entered the Trinidad Bay area. This anchor represents the observed coast.

stops.name: Point Grenville approaches
stops.note: The National Archives dates the expedition’s anchoring near Point Grenville to 14 July. A Spanish party conducted a possession ceremony. The ships subsequently stood offshore and separated.

stops.name: Columbia River mouth, offshore
stops.note: On the southbound survey Heceta saw the Columbia’s mouth. The ship remained offshore amid strong currents and crew illness. The southbound charted coast is omitted between station dates because the direct line would cross headlands.

stops.name: Monterey Bay
stops.note: The two survey vessels resumed the southbound passage after repairing and recovering at Monterey. The precise Santiago arrival day is omitted because the historical summaries differ.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: The expedition vessels returned to San Blas. Santiago’s second officer Pérez died at sea during the trip.

voyages.name: Bodega y Quadra and Mourelle’s Sonora voyage
voyages.summary: Sonora sailed with Santiago, then carried on independently into present-day southeastern Alaska and returned by California. Bodega commanded the schooner and Francisco Antonio Mourelle served as pilot.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: Trinidad Bay coast, California
stops.note: Sonora and Santiago reached the vicinity together after sailing from San Blas on 16 March.

stops.name: Point Grenville approaches
stops.note: Sonora anchored with Santiago. The schooner subsequently separated from Heceta’s ship.

stops.name: Kruzof Island approaches
stops.note: Bodega sighted Kruzof Island off present-day Sitka. The Navy study reports Sitka on 15 August. The marker is representative of the offshore approaches.

stops.name: Bucareli Bay entrance
stops.note: Bodega anchored near the entrance and sent Mourelle ashore to perform a Spanish claim ceremony. The exact site of the raised cross remains uncertain.

stops.name: Off Juan de Fuca Strait
stops.note: Sonora was off the strait. Winds prevented approach, so the schooner stood out to sea again. The intervening coastal waypoints are unresolved.

stops.name: Bodega Bay, California
stops.note: Sonora entered the bay, which Bodega initially believed to be San Francisco Bay.

stops.name: Monterey Bay
stops.note: Sonora reached Monterey and found Santiago there. The survey vessels then returned to San Blas.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: The two ships reached San Blas.

voyages.name: Arteaga and Bodega’s Alaska survey
voyages.summary: Arteaga commanded Princesa and Bodega commanded Favorita, with Mourelle as pilot. They sailed north together to survey southeastern Alaska and Prince William Sound. Their return dates and some survey dates differ between sources.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: The Spanish Navy study dates departure to 11 February. The National Archives account uses 12 February.

stops.name: Bucareli Bay entrance
stops.note: The vessels reached Bucareli Bay, where their crews surveyed different channels and anchorages. The marker represents the bay entrance. The reported departure times differ.

stops.name: Bucareli Bay survey region
stops.note: The Navy study dates the departure from Bucareli to 15 June. The National Archives account places the Favorita departure on 1 July. Both document substantial local survey activity before the ships proceeded toward Prince William Sound.

stops.name: Port Etches approaches, Hinchinbrook Island
stops.note: The vessels reached the Puerto de Santiago area according to this chronology. They staged the Spanish claim ceremony on 23 July. The archived synthesis distinguishes arrival in Prince William Sound from that ceremony.

stops.name: San Aniceto / Elizabeth Island approaches
stops.note: The ships anchored near San Aniceto at the approaches to Cook Inlet before exploring a nearby roadstead.

voyages.name: Bodega and Mourelle return in Favorita
voyages.summary: Favorita returned from the Alaska survey separately. The vessel refitted in San Francisco Bay before reaching San Blas.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: San Francisco Bay approaches
stops.note: Favorita reached San Francisco on 14 September. The San Francisco entry point depicts the approach, with repairs and provisioning in the Bay. The National Archives gives 30 October as the onward date.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: Favorita returned to San Blas first in the National Archives account.

voyages.name: Arteaga returns in Princesa
voyages.summary: Princesa reached San Francisco after the Alaska survey and returned to San Blas. The Navy study places San Francisco arrival a day after Favorita. The reported San Blas dates differ.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: San Francisco Bay approaches
stops.note: Princesa reached San Francisco on 15 September in the Navy chronology. The National Archives uses 14 September for both ships and gives a 30 October departure.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: The National Archives dates Princesa’s return four days after 21 November. The Navy study gives 30 November.

voyages.name: Martínez’s Princesa reconnaissance
voyages.summary: Martínez led a two-vessel reconnaissance of Russian activity, then sailed separately from Haro after the ships parted. The return dates in the Spanish Navy study and the Dictionary of Canadian Biography differ.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: Martínez sailed in Princesa alongside San Carlos, commanded by Haro.

stops.name: Trinity Islands approaches, south of Kodiak
stops.note: Princesa reached the Trinity Islands area. The Navy chronology has Haro rejoin there on 2 July before both vessels headed west on 5 July.

stops.name: Unalaska Bay region
stops.note: The official-history chronology places both ships at Unalaska in early August. The expedition gathered information on Russian plans and obtained supplies.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: The Navy study dates Princesa’s return to 5 November. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography places his return or report at San Blas on 5 December.

voyages.name: Haro and Narváez’s San Carlos reconnaissance
voyages.summary: The San Carlos and its pilot José María Narváez investigated Russian settlements. The ship’s stops differed from the expedition flagship’s after the vessels separated.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: Haro commanded San Carlos, known as El Filipino. The vessel left New Spain with Martínez in Princesa.

stops.name: Three Saints Bay, Kodiak Island
stops.note: The ship party contacted Russian commander Evstrat Delarov. José María Narváez helped make contact with the Kodiak fur-trade establishment.

stops.name: Unalaska Bay region
stops.note: Haro’s vessel reached the Unalaska region, where the crews found another Russian establishment. The Navy study gives this date for both vessels.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: The Navy study dates Haro’s return ahead of the flagship.

voyages.name: Martínez’s Nootka expedition
voyages.summary: Martínez returned with orders to occupy Nootka Sound. At Yuquot he built a Spanish post and seized foreign vessels, sparking an international dispute. The date of departure from Nootka differs by one day across sources.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: Martínez sailed in Princesa for Nootka Sound.

stops.note: Princesa anchored at Yuquot and supported a temporary occupation. Martínez dismantled and abandoned the Spanish post in late October. The National Archives gives 30 October for the departure and the Navy study gives 31 October.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: Martínez reached San Blas with news that the site had been evacuated.

voyages.name: Haro’s Nootka supply voyages
voyages.summary: Haro reached Nootka during the occupation under Martínez. His supply voyage left for Monterey and the return attempt was turned back by storms.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: San Blas, Nayarit
stops.note: San Carlos departed in company with Princesa.

stops.name: Yuquot / Friendly Cove, Nootka Sound
stops.note: The National Archives gives 12 May for Haro’s arrival and 27 July for departure on a supply mission. The Navy study gives 11 May for arrival.

stops.name: Monterey Bay
stops.note: Haro departed Monterey on a resupply mission.

stops.name: Off Nootka Sound
stops.note: San Carlos approached the coast near Nootka. A storm drove the ship away and Haro turned back south.

voyages.name: Narváez’s first Juan de Fuca reconnaissance
voyages.summary: Martínez sent José María Narváez to inspect the entrance of the Strait of Juan de Fuca in the captured schooner Santa Gertrudis la Magna. He returned after a short reconnaissance.

stops.name: Yuquot / Friendly Cove, Nootka Sound
stops.note: Narváez sailed south after Martínez seized and renamed the Northwest America. The day of the strait sighting is omitted, so no track is drawn.

stops.name: Yuquot / Friendly Cove, Nootka Sound
stops.note: He returned to Nootka after observing the Strait of Juan de Fuca without a sustained survey.

stops.note: Eliza, Fidalgo and Quimper departed with troops and supplies to reoccupy Nootka Sound.

stops.note: The Concepción and San Carlos arrived offshore but a storm kept them from entering the sound.

stops.name: Yuquot / Friendly Cove, Nootka Sound
stops.note: Eliza and Fidalgo anchored at Friendly Cove. Eliza met Indigenous leaders and rebuilt the Spanish post at Yuquot.

voyages.name: Fidalgo’s 1790 Alaska survey
voyages.summary: Fidalgo separated from Eliza’s force and investigated Russian activity around Prince William Sound and Cook Inlet. He returned via Monterey after weather prevented return to Nootka.
voyages.precision: Schematic itinerary between selected dated anchors. Coordinates identify representative historical places. Dates follow the cited sources.

stops.name: Yuquot / Friendly Cove, Nootka Sound
stops.note: Eliza dispatched Fidalgo on 4 May. The exact sailing time was soon afterward. The anchor represents the dispatch from the occupied port.

stops.name: Orca Inlet, Córdova approaches
stops.note: Fidalgo put ashore and carried out a Spanish claim at Orca Inlet after encounters with Indigenous traders.

stops.name: Port Valdez
stops.note: Fidalgo reached the port he named for Spanish naval minister Antonio Valdés.

stops.name: Nanwalek approaches, Cook Inlet
stops.note: Fidalgo staged a ceremony near a Russian post after encountering Russian traders. The point represents the offshore vicinity of modern Nanwalek.

stops.note: Fidalgo reached San Blas after returning by Monterey.

voyages.summary: Manuel Quimper, with pilots López de Haro and Juan Carrasco, surveyed both shores of the strait. The route anchors the documented Neah Bay stay, trade and claim ceremony, and the failed approach to Nootka on the return.

stops.note: The crew of Princesa Real left Nootka. They called in Clayoquot Sound and surveyed the northern side of the strait before turning to its southern shore.

stops.note: Quimper anchored on 24 July. Makah residents and Spanish crews exchanged goods. Quimper’s men made a Spanish claim on 1 August and sailed out on 3 August.

stops.note: Wind and fog prevented entry, so Quimper continued to Monterey. The intervening California passage lacks day-level positions.

stops.note: The ship reached Monterey after the unsuccessful approach to Nootka.

stops.note: Eliza sailed in San Carlos with pilots Pantoja and Verdía.

stops.note: Eliza arrived ahead of the schooner. They later sent small-boat parties to survey channels and islands.

stops.note: San Carlos returned to the post. Storms separated the schooner, which diverted south.

voyages.summary: The schooner operated as a distinct survey unit during the Eliza expedition. Narváez surveyed the inside waters and returned to the flagship. Carrasco took over for the return, which was diverted to California.

stops.note: The schooner arrived after the flagship and sailed to survey Rosario Strait on 14 June.

stops.note: Narváez rejoined Eliza and moved to San Carlos on 24 July, leaving the schooner to Carrasco.

stops.note: Dionisio Alcalá Galiano and Cayetano Valdés sailed to complete the survey of Juan de Fuca Strait.

stops.note: The National Archives reports that the schooners reached Nootka on 11 May. A historical field guide gives 13 May for arrival at Friendly Cove. The schooners left for Neah Bay on 5 June.

stops.note: The Spanish schooners met Vancouver’s boat party and exchanged survey information. They then continued into Burrard Inlet.

stops.note: The schooners passed Beaver Cove and sailed along Broughton Strait to anchor near Sisiaquis.

stops.note: The schooners rounded Cape Scott and returned to Nootka on 31 August. The headland passage is described without a day-level intermediate position.

voyages.summary: Fidalgo sailed in Princesa to establish a seasonal Spanish post at Neah Bay. Makah residents traded with the crews and later dismantled the outpost. Fidalgo returned to Nootka on Bodega’s orders.

stops.note: Fidalgo left directly for the Strait of Juan de Fuca.

stops.note: Fidalgo returned with the personnel and movable resources of the post. He took command at Nootka on 2 October.

voyages.summary: After Cook’s death, Clerke led a second attempt through Bering Strait. Ice blocked the northern passage. His last illness ended off Kamchatka on 22 August; the next dated port visit belongs to the surviving expedition under Gore.

stops.name: Avacha Bay, Kamchatka
stops.note: The ships repaired and provisioned in the bay. This is a regional anchorage, not a fixed mooring throughout the stay.

stops.name: Diomede Islands, Bering Strait
stops.note: The ships approached the narrow strait between Asia and America.

stops.name: Arctic pack edge, observed noon position
stops.note: King gives 70°26′N, 194°54′E at noon; this is not the farther-north position reached the next morning.

stops.note: Southward passage through Bering Strait.

voyages.summary: Gore and King brought Resolution and Discovery home after Cook and Clerke died. The ships called at Macao, islands near Southeast Asia and the Cape before returning through the North Atlantic. Narrow passages without sufficient fixes remain gaps.

stops.name: Macclesfield Bank

stops.name: Off Pulo Sapata
stops.note: Regional offshore reference for the sighting of Pulo Sapata, southeast of the island; not a landing.

stops.name: Pulo Condore, sheltered anchorage
stops.note: The crews obtained wood and provisions before sailing on 28 January.

stops.name: Prince’s Island, Sunda Strait
stops.note: Resolution rejoined Discovery at Prince’s Island on 14 February. Both prepared to sail; the attempt on 18 February was interrupted before getting away the next morning.

stops.name: Indian Ocean, south of Java

stops.name: South Atlantic, observed position

stops.name: Atlantic equator crossing

stops.name: Stromness, Orkney

stops.name: The Nore, Thames estuary

voyages.name: Orellana and Carvajal · Amazon descent and larger brigantine return
voyages.summary: The separately commanded river party continued downstream after leaving Gonzalo Pizarro. Carvajal describes exchanges, forced provisioning and violent attacks on Indigenous river communities. Selected confluences and the ocean exit precede the larger brigantine’s distinct arrival at Cubagua; the smaller vessel arrived two days earlier.
voyages.precision: Selected dated observations at representative historical places; unsupported travel between anchors is an explicit gap. Connections between supported observations are schematic.

stops.name: Rio Negro–Solimões confluence region
stops.note: Carvajal saw a dark-water tributary enter from the left on the Saturday before Trinity Sunday. Medina identifies the day as 3 June. This marks the confluence region, not a recovered vessel fix.

stops.name: Madeira–Amazon confluence region
stops.note: After the Corpus Christi episode and a rest day, the party passed a large tributary entering from the right. Medina identifies it as the Madeira and dates the passage to 10 June.

stops.name: Amazon northern outlet, Atlantic transition
stops.note: Carvajal explicitly dates the exit to 26 August but also calls it Saint Louis’s day, normally 25 August. The numeric day is retained as a qualified reference. Both brigantines left the river; they separated offshore on the feast of the Beheading of Saint John, without a known position.

stops.name: Nueva Cádiz, Cubagua — larger brigantine arrival
stops.note: Carvajal and Orellana arrived in the larger brigantine on 11 September after difficulty escaping the Gulf of Paria. They found the smaller brigantine already present. Paria passage dates are relative and no invented daily positions are supplied.

voyages.name: Champlain and Indigenous guides · Great Lakes journey and return
voyages.summary: Champlain’s own party traveled through the Ottawa–Nipissing–French River corridor to Wendat country, joined an unsuccessful allied campaign, wintered with his hosts and returned via Québec to France. The earlier Le Caron party and the detached interpreter’s travels remain distinct. Unlocated war, hunting and winter legs are gaps.
voyages.precision: Selected dated observations at representative historical places; unsupported travel between anchors is an explicit gap. Connections between supported observations are schematic.

stops.name: Québec — departure for the interior
stops.note: Champlain departed Québec with two men to rejoin his Indigenous allies. Joseph Le Caron and an earlier French contingent had already gone ahead; this route follows Champlain’s later party.

stops.name: Montréal–Rivière des Prairies approach
stops.note: Champlain embarked with an interpreter, his attendant and ten Indigenous canoeists, then ascended by the Rivière des Prairies and Ottawa. The marker denotes the Montréal approach; the text does not specify a launch beach.

stops.name: Lake Nipissing
stops.note: The canoe party entered Lake Nipissing and was hosted by Nipissing people. Champlain reports a two-day stay, followed by the French River descent; only the directly dated arrival is plotted.

stops.name: Otouacha, southern Georgian Bay region
stops.note: After the French River and Georgian Bay canoe journey, Champlain reached the Wendat village he called Otouacha. This regional reference does not identify a particular archaeological site.

stops.name: Carhagouha, Wendat country
stops.note: Champlain was present when Joseph Le Caron celebrated mass at Carhagouha. Champlain’s party then departed on 14 August to visit other Wendat villages en route to Cahiagué.

stops.name: Cahiagué, Wendat country near Orillia
stops.note: Champlain arrived at the Wendat assembly place on 17 August. He describes the village departure on 1 September, after which the allied force traveled toward Haudenosaunee country. The intervening campaign is represented separately at month precision.

stops.name: Cahiagué — return from the campaign
stops.note: After the unsuccessful attack, hunting and winter travel, Champlain returned to his Wendat hosts. Slafter’s note cites the 1632 account for 23 December and identifies the village as Cahiagué. Later winter visits are not represented as one uninterrupted stay.

stops.name: Falls of Saint Louis, Montréal — return departure
stops.note: After returning from Wendat country near the end of June, Champlain departed the Falls of Saint Louis with his host Darontal. The upstream return is not interpolated across the winter.

stops.name: Québec — return and onward departure
stops.note: Champlain reached Québec on 11 July and remained while repairs and construction proceeded, leaving in barques on 20 July for Tadoussac.

stops.name: Tadoussac — Atlantic embarkation
stops.note: Champlain’s barques reached Tadoussac on 23 July. He embarked in Pont-Gravé’s ready vessel and sailed for France on 3 August; the Atlantic passage has no intermediate fixes here.

stops.name: Honfleur — return to France
stops.note: Champlain dates his arrival in Honfleur to 10 September 1616, completing the return after the inland expedition and winter in Wendat country.

voyages.name: Alarcón’s San Pedro and Santa Catalina · maritime support expedition
voyages.summary: Alarcón sailed separately from Coronado’s overland force, adding San Gabriel en route. At the Colorado mouth he left the ships and used small boats upriver. The dated sea anchors do not place the ocean vessels at any proposed upstream limit.

stops.name: Acapulco, probable departure port
stops.note: Alarcón’s letter dates departure with San Pedro and Santa Catalina to 9 May but does not name the port. Winship identifies Acapulco as probable. Intermediate calls at Santiago and Guayabal are narrated without dates.

stops.name: Colorado River mouth — ship/boat separation
stops.note: At the head of the Gulf the ships remained behind while Alarcón and twenty men began a two-boat ascent on 26 August. The point marks the delta region and the change of party, not a recovered anchorage.

voyages.name: Alvarado and Padilla · separate reconnaissance to Tiguex
voyages.summary: Hernando de Alvarado and Juan de Padilla left Coronado’s Zuni headquarters and traveled by Acoma to the Rio Grande. The dated report establishes a separate reconnaissance; later Cicuye and Plains visits lack day-level anchors here.

stops.name: Háwikuh / Granada, Zuni
stops.note: The report places departure on the feast of the Beheading of Saint John, 29 August 1540. This is the detached Alvarado party, not a new movement of Coronado’s whole army.

stops.name: Tiguex, Middle Rio Grande region
stops.note: Alvarado reached the river on the evening before the Nativity of Mary, whose feast is 8 September. He subsequently received representatives from nearby Pueblo communities. The record denotes the region near Bernalillo, not a firmly located camp.

voyages.name: Alexei Chirikov’s St. Paul · independent North Pacific voyage
voyages.summary: St. Paul separated from Bering’s St. Peter and reached the southeast Alaskan coast independently. Two boat parties disappeared after approaching shore. The ship returned through the Aleutians with many men suffering from scurvy. Dates retain the published Russian Old Style convention.

stops.name: Petropavlovsk harbor, departure
stops.note: Chirikov distinguishes departure from the inner harbor on May 29 from departure to sea on June 4.

stops.name: Avacha Bay roadstead, departure to sea
stops.note: The two ships waited in the roadstead before putting to sea. Their later separation is not assigned a guessed ocean coordinate.

stops.name: Southeast Alaska, offshore of Cape Addington
stops.note: The journal records sighting the coast early on July 15 and a noon latitude near 55°36′. The editor identifies Cape Addington and Coronation Island from bearings. This is a shipboard observation.

stops.name: Southeast Alaska, Lisianski Strait approach
stops.note: Savelev and three companions were sent to look for Dementiev’s missing party. Bertholf uses the observed 57°50′ latitude and bearings to identify the Lisianski approach; other localities have been proposed. The marker belongs to St. Paul offshore.

stops.name: Adak Island, south-coast anchorage
stops.note: The journal entry describes visits by Unangax̂ men in skin boats. Bertholf’s later reconstruction describes the meeting on September 10. The date follows the journal heading, retaining the disagreement.

stops.name: Agattu Island, eastern offshore approach
stops.note: Editorial identifications connect the observed coast to Agattu, Semichi and Attu. Bertholf’s reconstruction places the sighting the morning after September 21; the journal-heading date is retained with uncertainty.

stops.name: Petropavlovsk harbor, return
stops.note: The journal and report date St. Paul’s move into the inner harbor to October 12, distinct from the earlier entrance to Avacha Bay.

voyages.name: Matonabbee, Samuel Hearne and companions · Coppermine journey
voyages.summary: Matonabbee led Hearne from Hudson Bay to the Coppermine River and back by Great Slave Lake. Indigenous women’s provisioning and transport work and knowledge from communities sustained the journey. Hearne’s later published account also records the killing of Inuit at Bloody Fall before the river-mouth survey; those descriptions are attributed to him.

stops.name: Prince of Wales Fort, Churchill River
stops.note: Hearne began his third attempt under Matonabbee’s guidance. The party traveled mainly on foot, using sledges and small canoes as conditions required.

stops.name: Coppermine River mouth, Arctic coast
stops.note: Hearne says the survey to the river mouth began on July 17 and was completed around 1 a.m. on July 18, after the violence at Bloody Fall. The party then began its return.

stops.name: Great Slave Lake, northern shore east of North Arm
stops.note: The party reached the north side of what Hearne called Athapuscow Lake. Tyrrell identifies Great Slave Lake, somewhere east of the North Arm entrance, rather than modern Lake Athabasca.

stops.name: Prince of Wales Fort, return
stops.note: After a June 29 river crossing and camp about ten miles from the factory, Hearne records reaching the fort next morning.

voyages.name: John Rae, William Ouligbuck and companions · Boothia sledge survey
voyages.summary: Rae’s land party crossed from Repulse Bay toward Boothia with Inuit assistance and surveyed part of its western coast. Ouligbuck interpreted and Mistegan made a separate reconnaissance farther north. Inuit travelers supplied information about Franklin’s crews. These mapped positions belong to Rae’s party.

stops.name: Pelly Bay region, observed camp

stops.name: Beecher River region, observed snow house
stops.note: Two Inuit travelers joined and guided the party. One related information about white men who had died far to the west. Rae placed the night’s river-bed snow house at 68°29′ N, 90°42′42″ W.

stops.name: Repulse Bay / Naujaat, return
stops.note: The party reached its winter home at 5 a.m. on May 26. Further Inuit accounts and expedition relics were obtained before the August boat return.

voyages.name: John Rae and companions · boat return to York Factory
voyages.summary: Rae returned down western Hudson Bay after further conversations with Inuit at Repulse Bay. Ouligbuck left the party at Churchill. Selected port dates do not reconstruct the difficult passage through packed ice in Frozen Strait.

stops.name: Churchill River entrance

stops.name: York Factory
stops.note: The party landed at York Factory during the forenoon of August 31.

stops.name: Brest roadstead

stops.name: Montevideo Bay

stops.name: Table Bay, Cape of Good Hope

stops.name: Ascension Island, northwest anchorage

stops.name: Saint-Malo

stops.note: A regional west-coast reference, not an identification of a precise historical mooring. The narrative records taking a friar hostage to obtain provisions.

voyages.name: Joshua Slocum · Spray circumnavigation
voyages.summary: Slocum’s published account follows Spray from Boston through Atlantic crossings, Brazil and the Río de la Plata, a difficult Magellan Strait passage, the Pacific, Australia, the Indian Ocean and the Caribbean return. Newport marks the circumnavigation’s return on 27 June 1898; the final 3 July Fairhaven homecoming is also shown. Captain Howard accompanied the local Montevideo–Buenos Aires excursion described in the book.
voyages.precision: Selected source-dated anchors, with approximate modern port, cape or island reference coordinates. Every intervening unsurveyed track is an explicit gap; markers are not navigational fixes. Connections between supported observations are schematic.
